Hay dos patrones elementales: (a) 'S o '(C)V́ ['ʔú] /'u/ 'mezclar' ['tá] /'ta/ 'pasto' (b) S'S o (C)V̀'(C)V́ [ʔò'á] /o'a/ 'chucha' [wɛ̀ɛ'kɨ́] /wɛ'kɨ/ 'danta'. El grupo acentual tiene dos niveles tonales determinados por el acento: el tono alto (´) siempre aparece en sílaba acentuada y el tono bajo (`) en sílaba inacentuada. [...] [p.111] El acento doble aparece en grupos acentuales con una secuencia de dos o más sílabas acentuadas. Su posición es predecible: si el grupo acentual termina en sílaba acentuada, el acento doble cae en la primera de las sílabas acentuadas; si el grupo acentual termina en sílaba inacentuada, el acento doble cae en la última sílaba acentuada, o sea en la que precede a la inacentuada.
new_statements.translation: The accent group, in its basic form, is defined as an accented, isolable unit of one or two syllables. There are two elementary patterns: (a) 'S, i.e. '(C)V [/'u/ 'mix', /'ta/ 'grass'] (b) S'S, i.e. (C)V̀'(C)V́ [/o'a/ 'opossum', /wɛ'kɨ/ 'tapir']. The accent group has two tone levels determined by the accent: high tone always appears on an accented syllable and low tone on an unaccented syllable. [...] The double accent appears in accent groups with a sequence of two or more accented syllables. Its position is predictable: if the accent group ends in an accented syllable, the double accent falls on the first of the accented syllables; if the accent group ends in an unaccented syllable, the double accent falls on the last accented syllable, i.e. the one preceding the unaccented one.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Siriano is analysed as a tone-accent (pitch accent) system built on the 'accent group' (essentially root + suffixes). A basic accent group is one or two syllables: monosyllables are accented; disyllables are low-high, i.e. accented on the second (final) syllable. Accent is realised as high tone, unaccented syllables as low tone. When suffixes are added, roots of the 'first category' spread accent/high tone onto following syllables (giving runs of high syllables), roots of the 'second category' keep all added syllables low; within a run of accented syllables the main ('double') accent is on the first accented syllable if the word ends high, otherwise on the last accented syllable before the final low. Monosyllabic roots yield word-initial accent (/'si'gɨ/, /'kubąsą/), disyllabic roots second-syllable accent (/bi'ragɨ/, /do'a'bu'gɨ/), so surface accent position follows root shape and lexical root class rather than a fixed word edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: No secondary stress as such; multiple contiguous accented (high) syllables are all high, with one 'acento doble' (main prominence) whose position is predictable (first accented syllable if the group ends accented, else last accented syllable). At phrase level an 'acento principal' coincides with the accent of the last accent group (anticadent intonation) or with/before the first downstep (cadent intonation), pp.103-105.
new_statements.exceptions: (C)V1'V1 groups with optional glottal stop shift the accent one syllable to the right and develop a falling glide when suffixed (sect. 2.3.1.2, e.g. /ba'a/ 'eat' -> /baa'gɨ/); pattern (d) only with contracted identical vowels; some verb forms show morphophonemic 'modificaciones tono-acentuales' (p.125, e.g. /aari'giikubi/ -> /aa'riikubi/); /bą'sa'ka/ 'gente' noted as the only nasal-spreading exception; tonal glides were heard only when a female consultant whistled the patterns (fn.8).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'grupo acentual' (root plus affixes, roughly the phonological word), nested inside the 'grupo fónico' (intonation unit) where a phrase-level main accent is assigned; data from San Pablo, río Paca, Vaupés, collected 1975; forms cited are isolated words and short utterances.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Siriano as spoken at San Pablo and along the río Paca, Comisaría del Vaupés, Colombia (data 1975, ~200 speakers); this is the language-level siri1274 [sri], no separate dialect glottocode. Desano (desa1247) is its closest relative (89% per Barnes 1999) but is not the variety described.

new_statements.relation_note: Type differs: the catalog's existing statement (Nagler & Brandrup 1979, coded pitch accent) analyses an 'accent group' with one accented syllable whose high pitch is determined by the accent; Ni 2021 analyses the same H/L facts as a two-tone system with lexical tone (HH vs LH minimal pair) plus a separate, unformalized stress. Placement is compatible: both put the prominence (1979 accent/high tone; 2021 high tone and stress) on the second syllable of CV̀CV́ roots (1979 pattern S'S, e.g. [ʔò'á] 'chucha'; 2021 [mõhṍ] 'hand'). The 2021 statement gives no general stress rule, so it does not replace the 1979 accent rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Siriano is described as a two-tone language (H vs L, lexical: HH págɨ́ 'take down' vs LH pagɨ́ 'father'); stress is named as a third suprasegmental that interacts with tone, but no general stress-placement rule is given. The only placement statements are for disyllabic roots with identical-vowel sequences (LH pattern, glottal stop/fricative between the vowels): stress is assigned to the second syllable, the longer, high-toned vowel (mõhõ 'hand', boo-Ri 'dry'), and it stays on the root's second vowel when a suffix is added. The thesis explicitly leaves metrical structure and the tone-stress interaction for future work. (The 'ɨ' in the quoted forms is rendered as '0' in the PDF text layer.)
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the analysis is called preliminary and covers only identical-vowel roots. When the object marker -Re attaches to waí 'fish', the high tone moves from the root's second vowel to the suffix ([waiʔRé], p.36) - a tone shift, not framed as stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Ni 2021 describes Siriano [sri] as spoken in the Vaupés region (Brazil/Colombia) from data collected by Wilson de Lima Silva; no dialect is named. Nagler & Brandrup 1979 is the Colombian ILV description. Same language, no variety distinction stated.

readall_conflicts: The two primary descriptions differ in type, not in placement. Nagler & Brandrup 1979 (existing catalog statement, coded pitch accent) describe an accent group of one or two syllables with two pitch levels 'determined by the accent' (high always on the accented syllable, low on the unaccented one; basic patterns 'S and S'S, p.106). Ni 2021 calls Siriano a two-tone language with lexical H/L tone (HH págɨ́ 'take down' vs LH pagɨ́ 'father', p.30), names stress as a separate suprasegmental that 'interacts' with tone (pp.10, 26), and locates stress only on the second, longer, high-toned syllable of identical-vowel roots (pp.39-40); it states no general stress rule and defers metrical structure to future work (p.96). Second-hand sources split the same way: Barnes 1999 (Tucano chapter) groups Siriano with the Tucanoan 'accent, or pitch accent' systems that allow two contiguous equally accented high syllables, while SAPHON codes Siriano 'Suprasegmental: Tone' after Criswell & Brandrup 2000 (not opened; print only). The HH pattern of Ni 2021 corresponds to the 1979/Barnes contiguous-high-syllables case, so the disagreement is analytic (accent vs tone), with the prominent syllable in CV̀CV́ roots the same in both.
